analysis.one_liner: Requires large electric utilities to gradually supply 20% of their power from renewable sources by 2027.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its energy subcommittee for nearly two years and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required retail electric suppliers selling at least 1 million megawatt-hours a year to obtain renewable energy credits covering a growing share of their sales — 1% in 2008, rising to 20% by 2027 and through 2037. Utilities could meet the target by generating renewable power themselves, buying or trading credits, borrowing against future credits, or buying credits from the Energy Department at a capped price. Money from those sales would fund state renewable energy grants and low-income energy assistance and weatherization.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary electricity customers get cleaner air and a power mix increasingly free of fossil fuels, with a hard cap on compliance costs. Low-income households get energy assistance and weatherization funded from credit sales. Renewable energy developers gain a guaranteed national market. Communities on Indian land and on-site generators earn extra credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electricity customers and renewable energy developers

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a graduated national requirement: 1% of sales from renewables in 2008, rising one point per year to 20% in 2027 and staying there through 2037.
A cost cap protects consumers: any utility can buy compliance credits from the Energy Department at no more than 3 cents per kilowatt-hour, limiting how much of the mandate's cost can reach bills.
Proceeds from credit sales are dedicated to state grants for renewable energy promotion and for energy assistance and weatherization services to low-income consumers.
The bill encourages federally-owned, municipally-owned, and cooperative utilities to join voluntarily, and leaves state renewable programs free to add stricter requirements on top.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil-fuel-heavy electric utilities must generate renewables or buy credits, and their prudently incurred incremental costs can be recovered from ratepayers, so electricity customers in coal-reliant regions would likely see modest bill increases.

drawbacks.text: Electric utilities may recover the full incremental cost of compliance from customers through their rates, so the mandate's cost ultimately falls on electricity bills rather than on utility shareholders.

Because the mandate applies nationwide regardless of local renewable resources, utilities in regions with little wind, sun, or biomass would rely on purchased credits or capped payments, raising costs where renewables are scarce.
Rural electric cooperatives, municipal utilities, and federal utilities are excluded from the requirement and only encouraged to participate voluntarily, weakening the standard's coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A national renewable standard of this scale would have shifted the power mix meaningfully toward renewables over three decades, with trading, borrowing, and a 3-cent compliance-price cap keeping costs contained, and credit-sale proceeds directed to low-income assistance. The main honest objection is that utilities can pass compliance costs through to ratepayers, so customers in renewable-poor regions pay something for cleaner power. The design is reasonably consumer-protective: the cost cap, four-year credit banking, and flexibility mechanisms prevent the mandate from being a blank check.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee a month later, and never moved again — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Udall introduced the bill on February 17, 2005, with six original cosponsors from both parties.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on March 22, 2005 to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
No further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 109th Congress: the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee vote and never reached the House floor.
The bill had gathered 36 cosponsors by the end, 31 Democrats, 4 Republicans, and 1 Independent, but that support was never tested in a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel-dependent electric utilities and coal generators are better off: no federal renewable mandate was imposed, and utilities were spared compliance costs and the requirement to buy credits or build renewable capacity.

sides.party_line_note: Support was mostly Democratic — 31 of 36 cosponsors were Democrats — but 4 Republicans and 1 Independent signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where the partisan split could be tested.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers (wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, landfill gas)
industries.note: A guaranteed national market: utilities must obtain renewable credits rising to 20% of sales, creating demand for new renewable generation. The bill adds bonus credits for Indian land (2x) and on-site generation (3x).
They would have had to build renewable capacity or buy credits at up to a capped price, and their product's market share would shrink year by year. Stopping the bill preserved their position.
Compliance is a cost, but the bill guarantees recovery of prudently incurred incremental costs from ratepayers, so shareholders are shielded while customers bear the expense.

industries.industry: Rural electric cooperatives and municipal utilities
industries.note: Excluded from the definition of a covered retail electric supplier and only encouraged to participate voluntarily, they would avoid the mandate's costs that other utilities and their customers bear.
